Jerome Robbins was an American choreographer and director who bridged classical ballet and Broadway, creating movement that was both technically precise and dramatically alive. Born in nineteen eighteen in New Jersey as Jerome Rabinowitz, he studied under various teachers and danced with the Ballet Theatre, now known as American Ballet Theatre. He created Fancy Free in nineteen forty-four, a ballet about three sailors on shore leave that became an instant classic and launched the jazz-ballet idiom. In nineteen forty-eight, he co-founded New York City Ballet with George Balanchine and served as associate artistic director, creating ballets including Dances at a Gathering and In the Night. He choreographed the Broadway musicals West Side Story in nineteen fifty-seven and Fiddler on the Roof in nineteen sixty-four, both landmark achievements that transformed musical theater's relationship to dance. He won three Tony Awards and two Academy Awards, his choreography for the West Side Story film in nineteen sixty-one setting a new standard for dance on screen. He developed a theatrical vocabulary that combined classical ballet technique, contemporary movement, and vernacular idioms into a seamlessly integrated storytelling language. As a director as well as choreographer, he understood dance as part of the total theatrical experience rather than an interpolated specialty.
